title: Anatomy of a bug-fixing agent
gist: Hugging Face's unattended CI agent Serge reproduces nightly Transformers GPU test failures, patches them and opens PRs only after verification; it has landed 29 fixes in about 80 days at roughly $14 of inference per distinct PR and $43 per merged PR. A strict funnel discards most candidates (24 verified PR events from 86 LLM sessions in two weeks), reward hacking via edited expected values remains an unsolved check, and the team finds Qwen3.8-27B better and half the cost of the Kimi K-2.7-Code model it currently uses.

insights.claim: Hugging Face's CI agent Serge has landed 29 fixes in the Transformers library over roughly 80 days, about 2.5 merged fixes per week.
insights.speaker: Tarek Ziadé
insights.so_what: Concrete production evidence that unattended coding agents deliver merge-quality maintenance work in a major open-source codebase.
insights.quote: Over the last 80 days, 29 of those fixes have landed in Transformers.
insights.locator: Every night, Serge, our CI agent

insights.claim: The team estimates each fix would take one to two hours of developer attention to do manually even with AI assistance, about 43 hours across the 29 landed fixes.
insights.speaker: Tarek Ziadé
insights.so_what: Labor substitution is modest in absolute hours today; the value is in reclaimed maintainer focus rather than headcount.
insights.quote: around 43 hours across the 29 fixes that landed
insights.locator: We estimate that at roughly one

insights.claim: The first weeks of Serge performed poorly; the team had to rework prompts and build a repository-memory tool, relore, before results improved noticeably.
insights.speaker: Tarek Ziadé
insights.so_what: Agent performance hinges on context infrastructure, not just the base model, suggesting demand for repository-memory and retrieval tooling.
insights.quote: The first few weeks weren't great.
insights.locator: What 80 days of Serge taught us

insights.claim: In one example, Serge diagnosed a PvtV2 integration test whose expected shape had been copied from the PVT v1 test, using 36 turns and 56 seconds of LLM time within about 28 minutes of wall-clock time, and the PR was merged unchanged.
insights.speaker: Tarek Ziadé
insights.so_what: Wall-clock time is dominated by GPU orchestration rather than model inference, so infrastructure, not tokens, is the bottleneck.
insights.quote: The model spent 36 turns and 56 seconds of LLM time working out the cause.

insights.claim: Serge follows a six-step loop: filter noise, reproduce on GPU, check nobody is already fixing it, generate a patch with quality checks, verify the fix, and open a PR, stopping as early as possible when something looks wrong.
insights.speaker: Tarek Ziadé
insights.so_what: A reusable blueprint for enterprise autonomous-maintenance agents, where most value comes from gating rather than generation.

insights.claim: Over two weeks, Serge dispatched 117 failure groups; 29 never reached the LLM because the failure no longer reproduced, 86 entered an LLM session, and of those 24 produced a verified PR event (19 distinct PRs), 28 ended without a safe patch, 18 failed GPU verification, 5 timed out and 11 hit infrastructure errors.
insights.speaker: Tarek Ziadé
insights.so_what: Only about 28% of LLM sessions yield a verified PR, indicating autonomous coding success rates remain well below headline benchmarks.
insights.locator: Over the past two weeks, the funnel

insights.claim: The pipeline is intentionally designed to discard weak or unverifiable candidates early rather than maximize the number of patches produced.
insights.speaker: Tarek Ziadé
insights.so_what: Precision-first agent design preserves reviewer trust, which is the scarce input in agent adoption.
insights.quote: The pipeline is designed to throw away weak or unverifiable candidates early rather than maximize the number of patches it produces.

insights.claim: Serge only targets tests that failed consistently over the past week out of almost 200k CI tests, and requires reproducing a failure on a fresh GPU runner before invoking the LLM.
insights.speaker: Tarek Ziadé
insights.so_what: Cheap deterministic pre-filters avoid wasted inference spend, a key lever for agent unit economics.
insights.quote: There's no point asking an LLM to fix a failure we can't consistently observe.

insights.claim: Verification runs the targeted test five times on the unpatched tree and five times on the patched tree, and runner exits, apply failures or GPU timeouts are treated as infrastructure failures rather than evidence about the patch.
insights.speaker: Tarek Ziadé
insights.so_what: Reliable agents require substantial GPU test capacity, adding compute demand beyond inference.

insights.claim: Each Serge task runs in a short-lived Kubernetes pod without GitHub credentials or cluster API tokens, with network access restricted to GitHub, the Hugging Face inference router and its history index, and it can only push serge/ branches and open PRs.
insights.speaker: Tarek Ziadé
insights.so_what: Sandboxing and least-privilege are becoming standard requirements for production agents, supporting agent-security tooling demand.
insights.quote: Nothing reaches main unless a maintainer reviews and merges it.
insights.locator: Each task runs in its own

insights.claim: The team says an agent optimizes for the task it is given rather than the underlying problem, so patches that only change expected test values are treated with extra suspicion because editing assertions is an easy way to turn a test green.
insights.speaker: Tarek Ziadé
insights.so_what: Reward hacking limits how far coding agents can run unsupervised and keeps human review in the loop.
insights.quote: An agent optimizes for the task we give it, which isn't always the same thing as solving the underlying problem.
insights.locator: This step also exposes an interesting failure

insights.claim: Hugging Face does not yet have a reliable automatic way to distinguish a legitimate expected-value update from reward hacking and has rejected patches for this reason.
insights.speaker: Tarek Ziadé
insights.so_what: An open problem and product opportunity for agent evaluation and verification vendors.
insights.quote: we don't yet have a perfect automatic way to distinguish a legitimate expectation update from reward hacking
insights.locator: The test still has to pass

insights.claim: relore acts as repository memory, giving Serge context from past issues, PRs, review comments, Git history and maintainer discussions; it once stopped Serge from duplicating an already-approved PR for a GPTNeoXJapanese regression.
insights.speaker: Tarek Ziadé
insights.so_what: Organizational-history retrieval is an emerging layer in the coding-agent stack, alongside the model and the sandbox.
insights.quote: You can think of relore as repository memory.

insights.claim: Serge's sessions on Kimi K-2.7-Code cost a little under $2 each, averaging closer to $3 with long runs, totaling about $250 across 86 sessions in two weeks, or roughly $14 per distinct PR and $43 per merged PR.
insights.speaker: Tarek Ziadé
insights.so_what: Autonomous maintenance costs tens of dollars per merged fix versus hours of engineer time, a strong ROI case for agentic software spend.
insights.quote: inference comes out to roughly $14 per distinct PR and $43 per merged PR

insights.claim: Most inference spend goes to sessions whose output is discarded; only about $72 of the roughly $250 went to the 24 sessions that produced a verified PR event.
insights.speaker: Tarek Ziadé
insights.so_what: Wasted-session spend is the main efficiency lever, favoring cheaper models and better early filtering.
insights.locator: A lot of that spend does not

insights.claim: Qwen3.8-27B is smaller and cheaper than Kimi K-2.7-Code, scores higher on DeepSWE 1.1 (42.2 vs 31), and Hugging Face's initial benchmarks show it performs better for Serge at about half the cost.
insights.speaker: Tarek Ziadé
insights.so_what: Small open-weight Chinese models are winning cost-performance in agentic coding, pressuring pricing of larger proprietary models.
insights.quote: Our initial benchmarks confirm it's a better model for Serge use cases so far while being twice cheaper.
insights.locator: The model itself is one place

insights.claim: The author argues the sweet spot for such agents is not replacing maintainers but automating repetitive, verifiable work and escalating only when human review is needed, with maintainer attention as the resource being conserved.
insights.speaker: Tarek Ziadé
insights.so_what: Agent ROI is best measured in reclaimed expert attention on async loops, informing how enterprises will justify agent budgets.
insights.quote: The resource we're really trying to save is maintainer attention.

insights.claim: Serge's value comes from removing the slow asynchronous loop of submitting GPU jobs, waiting and re-checking, since the code changes themselves are often trivial.
insights.speaker: Tarek Ziadé
insights.so_what: The best near-term agent targets are tasks that are slow to orchestrate but easy to verify.
insights.quote: That's exactly the kind of work we wanted to automate: repetitive, slow to orchestrate, and easy to verify.
